docs.contenu:
🎯 Objectives
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
- Understand what an argumentative (opinion) essay is and how it is organised.
- Write a clear thesis statement and support it with reasons and examples.
- Structure your ideas into introduction, body and conclusion.
- Use linking words, opinion phrases and a formal tone to persuade your reader.

🔍 Warm-up
Imagine your school wants to ban mobile phones during class. Some students agree, others disagree. If you had to write your view, how would you convince the reader? You would not simply say "I think phones are bad." You would give reasons, examples and a clear plan. That is what argumentative writing teaches you to do.

I. WHAT IS AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
📘 Rules and definitions
An argumentative essay is a piece of writing in which you defend a clear position on a debatable topic. Its aim is to persuade the reader that your opinion is reasonable, using logical arguments and evidence rather than emotion alone. A good essay is balanced: it may mention the opposite view but shows why your side is stronger.

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
Argumentative writing usually uses the present simple for general truths (Pollution damages our health), modal verbs for opinion and recommendation (Governments should invest in clean energy), and the passive for a neutral tone (It is often claimed that...).

👀 Notes
Choose a position early and keep it throughout. Do not defend one side in the introduction and the opposite side in the conclusion; consistency is what makes an argument convincing.

II. THE STRUCTURE OF THE ESSAY
📘 Rules and definitions
A standard opinion essay has three parts: an introduction, a body of two or three paragraphs, and a conclusion.

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
- Introduction: present the topic, show it is debatable, and end with your thesis statement (your main opinion in one clear sentence).
- Body paragraphs: each paragraph defends one main idea. Start with a topic sentence, add an explanation, then give an example or evidence.
- Conclusion: restate your opinion in different words and end with a final thought, recommendation or question.

🛠️ Writing method: building the essay step by step
1. Analyse the question and decide your position (for or against).
2. Brainstorm three or four strong arguments; keep the best two or three.
3. Find an example for each argument (a fact, a personal experience, a general observation).
4. Plan the order: put your strongest argument last for maximum impact.
5. Write the introduction, then the body, then the conclusion.
6. Reread and check grammar, spelling, linking words and tone.

✏️ Worked example of a thesis statement
Topic: Should students wear a school uniform?
Weak thesis: Uniforms are okay.
Strong thesis: In my opinion, school uniforms should be compulsory because they reduce inequality, save time in the morning and create a sense of belonging.
Notice how the strong thesis states the opinion and previews the arguments.

III. LANGUAGE FOR PERSUASION
📘 Rules and definitions
Persuasive writing relies on connectors, opinion phrases and precise vocabulary to guide the reader through your reasoning.

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
- Giving your opinion: In my opinion, I strongly believe that, It seems to me that, From my point of view.
- Adding ideas: Firstly, Secondly, Moreover, Furthermore, In addition.
- Giving examples: For instance, For example, Such as, A good illustration is.
- Showing contrast: However, On the other hand, Nevertheless, Although, Whereas.
- Showing cause and result: Because, Since, As a result, Therefore, Consequently.
- Concluding: In conclusion, To sum up, All in all, All things considered.

✏️ Worked examples
- Firstly, uniforms reduce social pressure, since every student wears the same clothes.
- However, some people argue that uniforms limit self-expression.
- As a result, students can focus on their studies rather than on fashion.
- To sum up, the advantages of uniforms clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

👀 Notes
Vary your connectors. Repeating "and" or "also" in every sentence makes the essay flat. A well-placed "Moreover" or "Consequently" shows control of the language.

IV. TONE, EVIDENCE AND COUNTER-ARGUMENT
📘 Rules and definitions
A formal, respectful tone makes your argument credible. Evidence supports your claims. A counter-argument shows that you have considered the other side before rejecting it.

📝 Grammar patterns and usage
- Introduce a counter-argument: It is true that... / Some people claim that...
- Then refute it: Nevertheless, ... / However, this argument ignores the fact that...

✏️ Worked example of a counter-argument
It is true that mobile phones can be a useful learning tool. Nevertheless, in most classrooms they distract students far more than they help, which is why they should be switched off during lessons.

🛠️ Method: a reliable paragraph pattern (P.E.E.)
- Point: state your main idea (topic sentence).
- Explain: develop and clarify it.
- Example: prove it with a concrete illustration.
Following P.E.E. in every body paragraph keeps your writing organised and convincing.

⚠️ Common mistakes
- No clear thesis: the reader cannot tell what you think.
- Listing ideas without explaining or illustrating them.
- Using informal language, slang or text abbreviations in a formal essay.
- Repeating the same idea in different words instead of adding new arguments.
- Introducing a brand-new argument in the conclusion; the conclusion should close, not open.
- Writing "I think, I think, I think" in every sentence; vary your opinion phrases.

⭐ To remember
- One clear opinion, defended from start to finish.
- Structure: introduction with thesis, body with P.E.E. paragraphs, conclusion.
- Use varied connectors and formal opinion phrases.
- Support every claim with an example.
- Acknowledge the opposite view, then refute it politely.

🔗 Applications
Argumentation is the backbone of the bac essay, but it also serves you far beyond the exam: in letters to a newspaper, job applications, debates, and any situation where you must defend a decision. Learning to argue clearly in English gives you a voice that others will take seriously.

enonce.question: Write a short paragraph (5-6 sentences) expressing your opinion on the following topic: 'Should students wear uniforms at school?' Use at least one argument to support your opinion and one counter-argument to show balance.
Match the function to the connector. Which connector shows CONTRAST: 'moreover', 'however', or 'therefore'?
Name the three main parts of an argumentative essay, in order.
Rewrite this weak thesis to make it clear and specific: 'Sport is good.'

Read the following argument and identify the main opinion, supporting arguments, and counter-argument. Then, write a balanced response (8-10 sentences) using the structure: introduction, argument, counter-argument, and conclusion.

Argument: 'Social media should be banned for teenagers under 16 because it exposes them to cyberbullying and misinformation.'

Your task: Write a response either supporting or opposing this argument, using at least two supporting points.
Put these stages of a body paragraph in the correct P.E.E. order: Example, Point, Explain.
Choose a more formal alternative for the informal sentence: 'Phones are a big no in class, if you ask me.'
Complete the counter-argument with a suitable refutation connector: 'It is true that television can be educational. ___, most channels broadcast programmes with little real value.'
Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph defending this idea: reading books improves the imagination.
Improve this repetitive sentence by varying the opinion phrase: 'I think phones are useful. I think they help students. I think they save time.'

Write a persuasive letter (10-12 sentences) to your school principal arguing for or against the idea of extending school hours. Use at least three arguments to support your opinion. Include an introduction, body paragraphs with arguments, and a conclusion. Use formal language and proper letter format (date, salutation, closing).

Example format:
[Your Name]
[Your Class]
[Date]

Dear Principal [Name],

[Your letter]

Sincerely,
[Your Name]
Write a full introduction (three to four sentences) for an essay on the topic: 'Should teenagers be allowed to have a part-time job?' End with a clear thesis statement.
Write one complete body paragraph (Point, Explain, Example) arguing that public libraries should stay open, using at least two connectors.
